input_signals.name: BoundedAccrualShareOfGrowth
input_signals.expression: RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), ADD(ABS(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), ABS(MA(capx, 3))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The composition of a firm's growth activity — the fraction contributed by non-cash working capital build-up rather than by real capital expenditure — predicts reversal, because paper growth unwinds while installed capacity does not.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the exploding accruals/capex ratio with a share that is mechanically bounded in [-1, 1], so small or zero capex can no longer generate extreme, sign-flipping cross-sectional ranks and the ordering is monotone in growth composition rather than in capex scarcity. Using a three-year capex average in the normalizer keeps the measure a statement about the firm's investment regime rather than one lumpy capital-budget year.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), add( abs( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ) ), abs( ma( capx, 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: BalanceSheetGrowthOutrunningWorkforce
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(COALESCE(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), 1), INDICATOR(SUB(GROWTH(at, 1), GROWTH(emp, 1)), 0))
input_signals.hypothesis: Accruals are most likely to be unproductive accounting expansion when the balance sheet grows faster than the workforce that must operate the assets; when headcount grows with assets, the same accruals reflect genuine scaling of operations.
input_signals.reasoning: Instead of subtracting a real-investment leg (whose own documented return relation runs the same negative direction and would cancel the accrual leg), employment growth enters purely as a state selector, so no leg is forced to carry a sign opposite to the established investment effect. It also removes the undefined growth-rate-of-working-capital problem by using an assets-scaled accrual level, and winsorizing bounds the continuous leg.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( coalesce( ratio( sub( ib, oancf ), at ), ratio( sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ), at ) ), 1 ), indicator( sub( growth( at, 1 ), growth( emp, 1 ) ), 0 ) )

input_signals.name: TotalAccrualShareOfGrowthActivity
input_signals.expression: RATIO(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), ADD(ABS(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp))), MA(capx, 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The fraction of a firm's total growth activity that is accrual accounting rather than real capital expenditure predicts reversal, and the broad accrual definition (earnings not backed by operating cash, including non-working-capital accruals) should capture more of the reversing component than the working-capital-only definition.
input_signals.reasoning: This holds the winning bounded-share architecture fixed and changes only the accrual numerator, so it directly tests whether total accruals or working-capital accruals is the right measure of "paper growth" in the composition ratio. The denominator adds strictly non-negative smoothed capex to the absolute accrual, so the signal stays bounded in [-1, 1] and cannot be hijacked by near-zero capex firms.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( coalesce( sub( ib, oancf ), sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ) ), add( abs( coalesce( sub( ib, oancf ), sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ) ) ), ma( capx, 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: CapexBeyondInternalCashFlow
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(MA(capx, 3), MA(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), MA(at, 3)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Capital formation that exceeds internally generated operating cash must be funded by external capital or supported by accrual-inflated earnings, and such unfunded real investment reverses far more than investment paid for out of realized cash flow.
input_signals.reasoning: Instead of adding two anomaly ranks, this differences the two themes inside a single asset-scaled quantity — a multi-year investment/cash-flow gap — so the interaction is the funding shortfall itself rather than a blend of investment and profitability signals. Three-year averaging captures the sustained regime rather than one lumpy capital-budget year, and COALESCE substitutes funds from operations (ib plus dp) only where the cash flow statement does not exist, preserving coverage without changing the economics.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( ma( capx, 3 ), ma( coalesce( oancf, add( ib, dp ) ), 3 ) ), ma( at, 3 ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: InorganicGrowthShare
input_signals.expression: RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), ABS(MA(aqc, 3))), ADD(ABS(ADD(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), ABS(MA(aqc, 3)))), MA(capx, 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Acquisition spending belongs economically on the same side of the ledger as accruals rather than with organic capital expenditure, because purchased growth arrives as revalued balance-sheet items instead of internally built capacity, so the share of growth activity that is accrual-plus-acquisition should predict reversal more strongly than the accrual share alone.
input_signals.reasoning: This makes a testable economic claim about *what counts as productive investment*, which is the core question of the theme, rather than restating the winning ratio: if the alpha strengthens, acquisitions are accounting growth; if it weakens, only organic capex has the disciplining property. Acquisitions enter in absolute smoothed form so that divestiture-driven negative aqc values cannot flip the numerator's sign.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( add( coalesce( sub( ib, oancf ), sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ) ), abs( ma( aqc, 3 ) ) ), add( abs( add( coalesce( sub( ib, oancf ), sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ) ), abs( ma( aqc, 3 ) ) ) ), ma( capx, 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: UnexpensedSoftAssetGrowth
input_signals.expression: RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, ppent), che), 1), ADD(ABS(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, ppent), che), 1)), MA(dp, 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Growth concentrated in non-cash, non-depreciable assets (receivables, inventory, intangibles, goodwill) escapes the income-statement discipline that depreciation imposes on real capital, so soft-asset expansion measured relative to the firm's expensing flow marks growth that must eventually be written off rather than depreciated.
input_signals.reasoning: The mechanism is new to the archive — expensing discipline rather than cash funding or investment direction — and depreciation is the natural cross-theme normalizer because it is the accounting rate at which real capital is consumed. Netting out cash prevents liquidity build-ups, which have the opposite return relation, from contaminating the soft-asset numerator, and the self-normalizing denominator keeps the measure bounded.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( delta( sub( sub( at, ppent ), che ), 1 ), add( abs( delta( sub( sub( at, ppent ), che ), 1 ) ), ma( dp, 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsPerUnitRealCapitalFlow
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: The right yardstick for accounting growth is the firm's total real capital flow — new investment plus capital consumption — so accruals per dollar of gross capital activity measure how much reported growth exists relative to the physical business actually being run.
input_signals.reasoning: This isolates the normalizer choice: the denominator is strictly positive and economically meaningful (gross capital turnover) instead of the self-normalizing |accrual| term, which mechanically compresses large accruals toward ±1 and tilts the short leg toward asset-light firms. Comparing its alpha with the bounded-share winner tells us whether the winning signal works through growth *composition* or through the low-capex tilt embedded in its denominator.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( coalesce( sub( ib, oancf ), sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ) ), add( ma( capx, 3 ), ma( dp, 3 ) ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: AccrualDominanceYearCount
input_signals.expression: TS_SUM(INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), at), RATIO(capx, at)), 0), 5)
input_signals.hypothesis: What predicts reversal is not the size of this year's accrual-led growth but how habitually a firm has expanded through accruals rather than capital expenditure; a firm that has been accrual-dominated in four or five of the last five years is running a chronically soft growth model, while one isolated accrual-dominated year is a transitory event.
input_signals.reasoning: This discards magnitude entirely and measures only the frequency of the cross-theme dominance state, so it answers the persistence-versus-event question with information that is genuinely orthogonal to the archive winner's level rather than by smoothing it. It also repairs the gen-0 failure of AccrualDominatedGrowthOnly, where the same dominance condition was multiplied by contemporaneous asset growth and produced a degenerate zero mass point; here every firm receives an informative integer score from zero to five.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ts_sum( indicator( sub( ratio( coalesce( sub( ib, oancf ), sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ) ), at ), ratio( capx, at ) ), 0 ), 5 )

input_signals.name: WCAccrualPerRealCapitalFlow
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: The reversing component of accounting growth is the working-capital build-up itself, measured against the scale of the firm's real capital activity; if this alone reproduces the archive's alpha, the accrual anomaly is about operating working capital rather than about depreciation policy.
input_signals.reasoning: This completes the missing cell of the 2x2 design grid (working-capital versus total accrual numerator, crossed with self-normalized versus gross-capital-flow denominator) and is the only clean way to attribute the −5% alpha of the two leading signals to a specific accrual component. Winsorizing guards the tail where capx+dp is small for asset-light firms, the instability the critic flagged.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), add( ma( capx, 3 ), ma( dp, 3 ) ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: UnamortizedIntangibleBuildup
input_signals.expression: RATIO(DELTA(intan, 1), ADD(ABS(DELTA(intan, 1)), MA(dp, 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Intangible and goodwill balances added to the books are capital that has been recognized but is largely shielded from systematic expensing, so firms whose intangible base grows large relative to their total amortization and depreciation flow are carrying asset values that must eventually be resolved through impairment rather than through orderly cost recognition.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the incorrect capx-minus-dp "decomposition" claim and instead tests a specific accounting-versus-real asset distinction: the growth in the least verifiable asset category measured against the firm's actual expensing capacity. It is not the net investment rate — the numerator contains no capital expenditure at all — and the impairment channel it targets is absent from the archive, where acquisitions entered only through aqc spending flows.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( delta( intan, 1 ), add( abs( delta( intan, 1 ) ), ma( dp, 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualVersusLaborExpansion
input_signals.expression: RATIO(WINSOR(RATIO(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), at), 1), ADD(ABS(WINSOR(RATIO(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), at), 1)), ABS(GROWTH(emp, 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Labor is the investment input that cannot be booked without being paid for, so a firm expanding its balance sheet through accruals while its workforce is flat is growing in a way no real operating commitment corroborates, whereas accruals accompanied by hiring reflect genuine scaling of the business.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the inventory numerator, which was a rediscovery of a published anomaly, with a real-investment yardstick that is orthogonal to capital spending and has been used in this archive only inside a failed binary gate. Both legs are dimensionless rates (accruals per asset and employment growth), so the self-normalized share is bounded in [-1,1] and comparable across capital-intensive and labor-intensive firms.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( winsor( ratio( coalesce( sub( ib, oancf ), sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ) ), at ), 1 ), add( abs( winsor( ratio( coalesce( sub( ib, oancf ), sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ) ), at ), 1 ) ), abs( growth( emp, 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsAgainstDecliningCashGeneration
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), DELTA(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 1)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Accounting growth is most likely to reverse when the cash engine behind it is already weakening: high accruals combined with a year-over-year fall in operating cash flow means reported expansion is being sustained precisely as its cash validation disappears.
input_signals.reasoning: Unlike the change in taxes payable, the change in operating cash flow is the same order of magnitude as total accruals, so this is a material perturbation that adds a dynamic cash-validation dimension rather than a negligible relabeling of the parent signal. It keeps the real-capital-activity denominator that already produces reliable alpha, so any improvement is attributable to the cash-deterioration term in the numerator.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( coalesce( sub( ib, oancf ), sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ) ), delta( coalesce( oancf, add( ib, dp ) ), 1 ) ), add( ma( capx, 3 ), ma( dp, 3 ) ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: TrendCashUnbackedAccruals
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), TREND(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters for the credibility of accrual-led growth is the direction of the cash engine over the investment cycle, not one noisy fiscal year, so a multi-year decline in operating cash generation should be a sharper disconfirmation of reported growth than a single-year drop.
input_signals.reasoning: This isolates the temporal form of the cash-validation term inside the current best signal, replacing a one-year difference with a three-year slope while holding numerator scale, deflator and winsorization fixed. Because year-to-year operating cash flow is volatile, the trend version should raise the slope reliability if the mechanism is a genuine cash-engine deterioration rather than a one-off accrual accounting artifact.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( coalesce( sub( ib, oancf ), sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ) ), trend( coalesce( oancf, add( ib, dp ) ), 3 ) ), add( ma( capx, 3 ), ma( dp, 3 ) ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: OwnHistoryExtremeOfPaperGrowth
input_signals.expression: TS_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), DELTA(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 1)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1), 5)
input_signals.hypothesis: Investors anchor on a firm's established growth model, so mispricing arises when cash-unbacked accrual growth reaches an unusual level *for that firm*, regardless of where the firm sits in the cross-section of capital intensity.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive has tested the level (strong), the one-year change (weak, t −1.6) and two-year persistence (strong), but never the firm's position within its own five-year distribution, which is the remaining temporal form and is naturally bounded in [0,1] — ideal for stable quantile sorts. A strong result would mean the effect is a within-firm surprise; a weak one would confirm that the cross-sectional level, not the firm-relative deviation, is what the market misprices.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ts_rank( winsor( ratio( sub( coalesce( sub( ib, oancf ), sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ) ), delta( coalesce( oancf, add( ib, dp ) ), 1 ) ), add( ma( capx, 3 ), ma( dp, 3 ) ) ), 1 ), 5 )

input_signals.name: NonCashCapitalGrowth
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ppegt, 1), capx), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Gross property, plant and equipment can rise for reasons that never involved a dollar of capital spending — acquired asset step-ups, capitalized overhead and interest, revaluations and consolidations — and this non-cash portion of capital growth is accounting growth wearing the clothes of productive investment, so it should reverse like an accrual while capex-backed capacity growth should not.
input_signals.reasoning: This moves the accounting-versus-real distinction inside the capital account itself, comparing the balance-sheet capital increase with the cash-flow-statement capital outlay, a construct no archive signal has touched and one that is not a decomposition of Sloan accruals. The deflator is the validated gross-capital-flow scale so the only new element is the numerator, and winsorization contains the retirement-driven negative tail.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( delta( ppegt, 1 ), capx ), add( ma( capx, 3 ), ma( dp, 3 ) ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: WorstOfTwoSoftGrowthChannels
input_signals.expression: MAX(RATIO(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), ADD(ABS(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp))), MA(capx, 3))), RATIO(DELTA(intan, 1), ADD(ABS(DELTA(intan, 1)), MA(dp, 3))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Growth quality is compromised if expansion is soft on *either* dimension — cash-unbacked working-capital accruals or a build-up of intangible assets shielded from amortization — so the firms that should be shorted are those failing at least one test, while the long leg should contain only firms whose growth is clean on both.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a union rather than an intersection of two channels that the archive has separately validated in different metrics (the accrual share carried the alpha at t −5.0, the intangible build-up carried the slope at t −3.9), and taking the maximum of two ratios already bounded in [-1,1] keeps the composite bounded and comparable without any deflator change. It replaces the rejected rescaling with a structural aggregation hypothesis whose failure would be equally informative: it would say the two channels are substitutes, not complements, and that intangible build-up simply does not reverse in tradable form.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: max( ratio( coalesce( sub( ib, oancf ), sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ) ), add( abs( coalesce( sub( ib, oancf ), sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ) ) ), ma( capx, 3 ) ) ), ratio( delta( intan, 1 ), add( abs( delta( intan, 1 ) ), ma( dp, 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AgedCapitalSoftGrowth
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), TREND(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), MUL(ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3)), RATIO(ppent, ppegt))), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: The same dollar of cash-unbacked accrual growth is far more dangerous in a firm whose productive base is already largely depreciated, because such a firm faces an imminent replacement bill it is not funding while it books soft revenue; scaling the deflator by the undepreciated fraction of the capital stock makes the signal larger exactly for those aged-asset firms.
input_signals.reasoning: Asset age (net over gross PP&E) is a new interaction dimension for this archive — every prior signal treated capital only through flows — and it enters as a strictly positive multiplier bounded between zero and one, so it rescales rather than re-signs the validated numerator and cannot create a sign conflict. It is not a recombination of two tested designs: the hypothesis is that vintage of installed capital moderates the reversal of accounting growth.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( coalesce( sub( ib, oancf ), sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ) ), trend( coalesce( oancf, add( ib, dp ) ), 3 ) ), mul( add( ma( capx, 3 ), ma( dp, 3 ) ), ratio( ppent, ppegt ) ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: DebtFundedSoftGrowth
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), TREND(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), ADD(DELTA(dlc, 1), DELTA(dltt, 1))), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Cash-unbacked accounting growth financed by new borrowing is the most fragile configuration, because the working-capital unwind arrives alongside a refinancing requirement, whereas the same accruals in a firm repaying debt are being absorbed by a strengthening balance sheet.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's two financing-conditioning attempts failed as binary gates (fmb +0.42 and +0.48) because gated-off firms piled up at zero; this puts the same economics into the numerator continuously and at a dollar magnitude comparable to the accrual term, which is the construction style that has consistently produced alpha here. Debt growth and accrual softness both predict low returns, so the legs reinforce rather than offset.

input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( add( sub( coalesce( sub( ib, oancf ), sub( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), dp ) ), trend( coalesce( oancf, add( ib, dp ) ), 3 ) ), add( delta( dlc, 1 ), delta( dltt, 1 ) ) ), add( ma( capx, 3 ), ma( dp, 3 ) ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: SoftGrowthWithDepreciationRelief

input_signals.hypothesis: Firms supporting reported growth with accruals often reach for a second accounting lever — slowing the rate at which they depreciate an unchanged capital base — and the dollars of expense thereby avoided belong in the same soft-growth numerator as the cash-unbacked accrual itself.
input_signals.reasoning: The added term is the depreciation-rate deceleration converted to dollars by multiplying through by the gross capital stock, so it is materially sized rather than a negligible perturbation, and it does not double-count the deflator: it depends on the *change in the depreciation rate*, not on the level of capex. This repairs the earlier depreciation-policy signal that produced a wrong-signed alpha (+2.5) when used as a binary gate on capital intensity, by moving the same accounting-choice idea inside the validated continuous numerator.

input_signals.name: CumulativeAccrualBloatCashValidated
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(TS_SUM(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), 3), SUB(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), LAG(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3))), ADD(TS_SUM(capx, 3), TS_SUM(dp, 3))), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Accounting growth accumulates: three years of accruals that have not been ratified by any three-year improvement in operating cash generation represent a stock of unconverted reported growth, and that stock should reverse more reliably than a single year's accrual flow.
input_signals.reasoning: Every archive signal has varied the *cash-validation* horizon while holding the accrual leg at one year; this is the untested dimension, and it is not a net-operating-asset rediscovery because the cumulative accrual is explicitly netted against the cumulative cash-flow improvement over the same window. Numerator and deflator are both three-year sums, so the ratio remains dimensionless and directly comparable to the one-year members of the family.
input_signals.author: proposer

input_signals.name: LeveragedSoftGrowth
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), TREND(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1), RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cash-unbacked accounting growth becomes a repricing event only when creditors are involved: a levered firm whose accruals reverse faces covenant pressure and forced retrenchment, while an unlevered firm simply absorbs the unwind, so the return consequence of soft growth should scale with the stock of interest-bearing debt.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a moderating-state hypothesis about *who bears the reversal*, not a rescaling of the softness measure — the debt-to-assets multiplier is a positive bounded weight, so unlevered firms are pushed to the middle of the sort rather than into a tail. It is distinct from the archive's DebtFundedSoftGrowth, which added debt *issuance flows* to the numerator and weakened the alpha; here leverage never enters the definition of softness, only its consequence.

input_signals.hypothesis: Firms defending reported growth sometimes stop replacing the capital they consume; the dollars by which capital spending falls short of depreciation are a real-side softness term that belongs alongside cash-unbacked accruals, because both flatter current earnings at the expense of future capacity.
input_signals.reasoning: This repairs the previously flagged harvesting idea with a one-sided construction: MIN(capx, dp) makes the term exactly zero for every firm investing at or above depreciation, so heavy investors are never penalised and the sign conflict with the investment anomaly disappears, unlike the earlier (dp − capx) term that rewarded low capex mechanically. It is a new numerator channel rather than another cell of the weight × numerator grid, and it is materially sized because maintenance shortfalls run into the same dollar magnitudes as annual accruals.

input_signals.hypothesis: An absolute solvency threshold, not a trend, is what condemns accrual-led growth: if operating cash flow does not even cover the depreciation of the assets in use, the business is consuming capital while reporting growth, and the accrual must reverse.
input_signals.reasoning: Every cash-validation term tested so far is relative — a change, a slope, a peak drawdown — whereas this is an economically absolute benchmark, the capital-consumption charge, and it is one-sided so firms comfortably covering depreciation contribute exactly zero rather than offsetting the accrual. That makes it conceptually distinct from the archive's drawdown and trend constructs while remaining in the numerator style that has produced every reliable alpha in this search.

input_signals.hypothesis: A firm reveals its attainable working-capital efficiency by its best year: the dollars of operating current assets it now carries in excess of what its most efficient historical conversion horizon would require are accumulated unconverted growth that should still be written off.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the working-capital counterpart of the cash-flow high-water-mark idea that the critic rated highest, and it differs substantively from the gen-8 overhang term, which benchmarked against the three-year *average* horizon and could therefore be negative and offsetting; benchmarking against the five-year *best* horizon makes the term non-negative and interpretable as recoverable slack. It closes the search with a construct that measures the stock of unconverted growth rather than its flow, using the firm's own demonstrated efficiency as the standard.
